title: Power Becomes the AI Bottleneck: Korea's Grid Pivot and North America's Next Industrial Opportunity
author: Naru
excerpt: AI data centers and semiconductor fabs are turning electricity, storage, water, and permitting into the new competitive layer of industrial strategy. Korea's response offers a useful signal for Canada and the United States.
body:
AI infrastructure is rewriting the clean-energy conversation. For Korea, Canada, and the United States, the constraint is no longer only model performance, chip supply, or capital. It is whether power systems can deliver large blocks of reliable, affordable, lower-carbon electricity quickly enough to make the next generation of data centers, semiconductor clusters, and automated laboratories bankable.

Introduction

For much of the last decade, clean energy was framed primarily as a decarbonization challenge. That frame is now incomplete. In 2026, electricity has become an industrial input as strategically important as chips, talent, land, and capital. The AI buildout is exposing a harder question for advanced economies: can their grids support the manufacturing and compute capacity they want to host?

AI data centers and semiconductor fabs require high-quality, around-the-clock power, long-term price visibility, water or advanced cooling strategies, transmission access, permitting certainty, and community acceptance. They also arrive on investment timelines that are faster than most new nuclear reactors, transmission corridors, pumped-storage projects, or interprovincial grid interties can be built.

The strongest common trend is not simply that AI uses more electricity. It is that energy infrastructure has become a competitive layer of AI industrial policy. Compute, clean power, grid resilience, advanced manufacturing, biotech innovation, and investment are converging into one market.

The new competitive question is not only which region has the best AI model. It is which region can deliver firm, scalable, lower-carbon power quickly enough to make AI-era industry investable.

Signals from Korea

South Korea is a useful lead indicator because its industrial ambition is explicit. The country is trying to expand semiconductor manufacturing, AI data centers, advanced manufacturing, and clean-energy exports at the same time. That creates a direct collision between industrial strategy and electricity planning.

On July 3, The Korea Times reported that Climate, Energy and Environment Minister Kim Sung-hwan said Korea should quickly review additional nuclear reactors to meet demand from semiconductor complexes and AI data centers. His reasoning was practical: semiconductor production needs stable electricity 24 hours a day, making it functionally similar to baseload demand. He said renewable energy alone would be difficult to rely on for this growth profile.

The signal sharpened on July 14, when The Hankyoreh reported that South Korea would consider new nuclear plants and SMRs in the 12th Basic Plan for Electricity Supply and Demand. Confirmed projects such as semiconductor clusters in Yongin and greater Jeolla, plus AI data centers, were described as needing an additional 30 gigawatts. Factoring in electric vehicles and building electrification, additional demand could exceed 50 gigawatts by 2040. Korea also reiterated a target of at least 100 gigawatts of renewable capacity by 2030, alongside nuclear power.

This is not only a debate about nuclear energy. It is a recognition that Korea's semiconductor and AI strategy cannot be separated from grid architecture. A fab is a long-term electricity obligation. A data center campus is a transmission-planning event. An AI cluster is a water, cooling, land, and local-acceptance challenge. Korea is moving from technology policy to infrastructure policy.

Storage is the second signal. On July 16, ESS News reported that South Korea's Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment signed agreements with nine companies for the country's first distribution-network energy storage support program. The initiative will put 4 MW / 20 MWh systems on 32 distribution lines in Honam and Jeju, where solar projects have faced interconnection queues and curtailment. The ministry expects roughly 700 MW of ESS by 2030, enabling an additional 1 GW of renewable interconnection capacity.

The third Korean signal is long-duration storage and water infrastructure. ChosunBiz reported on July 18 that Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power is accelerating a pumped-storage study in the Honam region, where solar growth has already stressed transmission and distribution capacity. KHNP is studying a mid-sized pumped-storage plant of more than 200 MW in renewable-rich areas. Honam's semiconductor cluster alone is expected to need 6.3 GW of power, and additional data centers would raise the requirement for continuous, high-quality electricity.

The commercial significance is clear. Korea is assembling a portfolio: renewables, nuclear, SMRs, distribution batteries, pumped storage, LNG transition options, water planning, and differentiated electricity pricing for AI data centers. For Korean companies, this domestic pressure can become a global advantage if it produces bankable products and operating models for markets facing the same constraint.

North American Perspective

North America is facing the same demand shock, but its institutional response is more fragmented. Canada, the United States, provinces, states, utilities, hyperscalers, and federal agencies are moving at different speeds.

Canada starts with a structural advantage: a relatively clean electricity system, deep hydro resources, nuclear expertise in Ontario, strong engineering talent, critical minerals, and established project-finance institutions. In May, the Prime Minister's Office announced consultations for a National Electricity Strategy designed to double the capacity of Canada's grid by 2050. The announcement said Canada already has an 80% clean grid and that electricity demand is expected to double by 2050.

For clean energy executives and investors, the key point is that Canada is trying to turn clean electricity into an economic-development platform. The strategy names generation, transmission, distribution, storage, grid modernization, interprovincial connections, workforce, and domestic manufacturing as pillars. That is climate policy, but it is also investment-attraction policy.

Yet Canada's AI infrastructure market is not developing evenly. The most visible project is in Alberta, where speed, land, gas infrastructure, and provincial support are outweighing the cleaner average national grid mix. On July 8, Meta announced its first Canadian data center, a 1 GW AI-optimized campus in Sturgeon County representing more than C$13 billion of investment. Meta said it would fully fund new generation and grid infrastructure and match the facility's electricity use with 100% clean and renewable energy.

The power-supply details show why this is an industrial-policy case study. Capital Power announced a long-term energy supply agreement for 250 MW of capacity and energy to support Meta's Sturgeon County data center, with load expected in the back half of 2028. The agreement is built around dependable, dispatchable generation and Alberta's ability to serve large-scale AI infrastructure. It illustrates a "bring your own power" approach for hyperscale loads: large customers fund new generation and grid infrastructure rather than relying entirely on existing system capacity.

The United States is moving through a different channel: federal land, national security, and dedicated on-site generation. On July 21, World Nuclear News reported that the US Department of Energy's National Nuclear Security Administration selected Amentum to enter negotiations for a phased lease at the Savannah River Site in South Carolina. The proposed project would establish a 1 GW AI data center supported by 2 GWe of dedicated on-site energy generation, initially using natural gas as a bridge to advanced nuclear energy.

The North American difference is market structure. Korea can move through national plans, state-linked utilities, and coordinated industrial policy. North America has more decentralized power markets. That can slow coordination, but it also creates many entry points for Korean innovators: provincial partnerships in Canada, utility pilots, behind-the-meter systems, SMR supply chains, battery safety, grid orchestration software, EPC partnerships, and industrial water solutions.

Connecting the Dots

These developments are occurring simultaneously because AI has turned infrastructure timing into a technology constraint. Compute demand is scaling in months. Power systems scale in years. Nuclear and transmission can take longer. Storage, gas turbines, advanced cooling, demand response, and grid software are therefore becoming bridge technologies between AI ambition and physical infrastructure.

The pattern is similar across Korea and North America. Governments are recognizing that AI and manufacturing are electricity-intensive industrial activities, not just software sectors. Companies are moving from buying power as a commodity to structuring energy as part of the project. Investors are underwriting sites based on time-to-power, grid reliability, permitting, water, and community risk. Regions are realizing that the economic prize includes supply chains around power electronics, transformers, batteries, nuclear components, construction, cooling, cybersecurity, and operations.

This is where Korea's experience becomes relevant to North America. Korean companies have deep capabilities in batteries, power equipment, EPC delivery, shipbuilding-derived modular construction, nuclear supply chains, digital grid platforms, and advanced manufacturing. Those capabilities map directly onto the constraints facing Canadian and US AI infrastructure.

The link to biotech is also important. Synthetic biology, AI drug discovery, precision fermentation, and automated labs are less electricity-intensive than gigawatt AI campuses, but they depend on the same infrastructure stack: reliable clean power, data-center access, robotics, temperature control, water systems, and resilient supply chains. As AI for biology moves from cloud modeling to automated experimentation and biomanufacturing, regions with credible power and industrial infrastructure will have an advantage.

Investment is following this logic. Capital is no longer looking only for the best algorithm or the cheapest megawatt-hour. It is looking for integrated infrastructure propositions: firm power, credible decarbonization, local benefits, skilled trades, permits, and optionality for storage, SMRs, hydrogen, or carbon capture.

Industry Implications

For startups, energy credibility becomes part of the product. AI, climate tech, and synthetic biology startups entering North America should be prepared to explain their infrastructure assumptions. If the product depends on large-scale compute, lab automation, fermentation, cold chain, or manufacturing, investors will ask about energy cost, availability, and resilience.

For enterprises, procurement will reward integrated partners. Utilities, data-center developers, manufacturers, and industrial landlords will want battery systems with safety cases, grid software with utility workflows, EPC partners with local compliance knowledge, and technology vendors that understand financing and permitting. Korean companies entering Canada should lead with project economics and deployment credibility, not only product specifications.

For governments, power strategy is now investment attraction. Canada can compete for AI and advanced manufacturing if it turns clean electricity into a coordinated market-entry advantage. That means faster interties, clearer rules for large-load connections, Indigenous and community partnership models, support for domestic grid manufacturing, and pathways for foreign technology partners to pilot locally.

For investors, the diligence lens changes. A data-center or advanced-manufacturing investment is not only a real-estate or technology deal. It is a power-development deal. Investors should diligence utility interconnection, capacity-market exposure, equipment lead times, cooling and water strategy, local political support, carbon accounting, and optionality for storage, SMRs, hydrogen, or carbon capture.

For Korean-North American partnerships, Canada is a practical test bed. Canada has clean power, mineral resources, AI talent, public funding tools, and a need to move faster. Korea has advanced industrial execution, battery and grid technology, nuclear supply-chain depth, and manufacturing discipline. The partnership opportunity can take the form of distribution-ESS pilots, Korean power-equipment manufacturing in Canada, joint SMR supply-chain work, critical minerals processing, and AI-lab infrastructure serving biotech and materials discovery.

Conclusion

What does this trend mean for North America? It means the AI economy will be shaped as much by energy and infrastructure execution as by software. Canada and the United States have enormous advantages: capital markets, hyperscaler demand, AI talent, nuclear and hydro assets, land, natural gas, critical minerals, and sophisticated utilities. Those advantages convert into durable economic value only if regions can build power capacity, transmission, storage, and community-supported industrial sites faster and more coherently.

For North American business leaders, the immediate opportunity is to treat power as a strategic platform. Data centers, semiconductor projects, AI-native laboratories, and biomanufacturing facilities should be planned around integrated energy roadmaps from day one. That includes bridge power, clean-energy matching, long-duration storage, demand flexibility, advanced cooling, water stewardship, and credible decarbonization pathways.

For Canada specifically, Korean innovation could have an outsized positive impact. Korea's battery companies, power-equipment manufacturers, nuclear suppliers, EPC firms, and grid-software developers have practical experience in dense industrial systems where reliability matters. Canada can use that experience to accelerate clean-energy deployment, strengthen critical-minerals-to-battery supply chains, support AI infrastructure without overburdening consumers, and build joint R&D platforms for SMRs, hydrogen, storage, carbon capture, and AI-enabled grid operations.

The actionable insight is straightforward: Canada should identify a small number of infrastructure corridors where AI compute, clean power, advanced manufacturing, and biotech can reinforce each other, then invite Korean firms into pilot projects with clear commercial pathways. Korea's domestic grid pivot is a warning about constraints, but it is also a blueprint for opportunity.

title: North American expansion: reading the 2026 signals for Korean innovators
author: Naru
excerpt: The macro backdrop for companies entering Canada and the U.S. is shifting. Here is how to read the signals — and what to do about them.
body:
North America in 2026 is not the same market it was even two years ago. Supply-chain realignment, friend-shoring incentives, and a wave of climate and AI capital have opened doors for innovators from Korea and beyond — but the bar for a credible entry has risen at the same time.

Enterprise buyers are more skeptical. Investors are more selective. Government programs reward companies that show up with a local footprint, not just a translated pitch deck. If you are planning a North American expansion this year, the question is not whether opportunity exists — it is whether you are reading the signals correctly.

Signal 1: Applied technology beats pure R&D

Funding and procurement across Canada and the U.S. increasingly favour technology that can be deployed, piloted, and commercialized within 12–18 months. Pure research milestones matter less than proof of local relevance: a pilot customer, a regulatory pathway, or a channel partner already in place.

For Korean companies with strong IP, this is an advantage — if you reframe the story from “our technology is advanced” to “here is how this solves a North American buyer’s problem today.”

Signal 2: Consolidation rewards localized vendors

Enterprise procurement teams are reducing vendor sprawl. That means fewer slots for new suppliers — but those slots go to companies that look and sound like credible local partners. Localization is no longer a marketing nice-to-have. It is a qualification criterion.

  • Website and sales materials written for North American buyers, not translated from Korean
  • Reference customers or pilots in Canada or the U.S.
  • Clear pricing, support, and compliance language
  • A named local contact or entity buyers can contract with

Signal 3: Capital is patient but selective

VC and strategic investment in clean energy, AI, healthtech, and advanced manufacturing remains active — but due diligence has tightened. Investors want to see a path to revenue in North America, not just market size slides. Strategic corporate investors, in particular, are looking for technology they can integrate into existing operations.

The companies that win in 2026 are not the ones with the best technology in isolation. They are the ones that arrive with a point of view about the North American customer.

What to do in the next 90 days

If you are evaluating a North American entry this year, start with three questions:

  • Who is the first buyer? Not a market segment — a specific persona, company type, or procurement category.
  • What proof do they need? Pilot structure, certifications, references, pricing model.
  • What must be built locally? Entity, partnerships, messaging, support — before you scale spend.

Most consultancies will hand you a market report and stop there. We stay until you have traction — because reading the signals is only useful if you act on them.

title: Canadian grants 101: how Korean startups can access IRAP and NRC programs
author: Naru
excerpt: A practical primer on Canada’s non-dilutive funding landscape — eligibility, programs, and how to position a competitive application.
body:
Canada’s innovation funding ecosystem is one of the most generous in the world for applied technology companies — but it is also nuanced, program-specific, and often misunderstood by companies entering from abroad. Programs like IRAP (Industrial Research Assistance Program) and the broader NRC (National Research Council) portfolio can meaningfully de-risk your first years in North America. The catch: you need to qualify, apply well, and understand what each program actually funds.

This guide is a starting point, not legal or financial advice. Every application depends on your technology, entity structure, and commercialization plan.

Why Canada first?

For many Korean and international innovators, Canada is a logical first North American beachhead: lower entry friction than the U.S. for some sectors, strong federal and provincial innovation programs, and a market large enough to validate product-market fit before a U.S. scale-up.

Grants and repayable contributions can fund R&D, hiring, commercialization, and market development — without diluting your cap table. That matters when you are still proving the model locally.

IRAP: what it is and who it is for

IRAP is delivered through the National Research Council and supports small and medium-sized Canadian businesses pursuing technology-driven innovation. Typical support includes:

  • Funding for R&D projects with clear commercial potential
  • Access to IRAP industrial technology advisors (ITAs)
  • Support for hiring technical talent in Canada

Key eligibility considerations for international companies: IRAP generally requires a Canadian incorporated entity actively conducting R&D in Canada. A Korean parent with a Canadian subsidiary — or a plan to establish one — is often the starting point. “We will incorporate later” rarely works; the entity and activity need to be real.

NRC and adjacent federal programs

Beyond IRAP, the NRC ecosystem includes specialized centres, collaborative R&D programs, and sector-focused initiatives in areas like AI, biotech, clean technology, and advanced manufacturing. Provincial programs (Ontario, BC, Quebec, and others) stack on top of federal support — SR&ED tax credits, regional development funds, and sector accelerators.

The landscape is wide. The mistake most companies make is applying to everything. The better approach: identify two or three programs that match your stage, sector, and entity structure — then build a coherent narrative across them.

How to prepare a competitive application

  • Canadian entity and local activity. Incorporation, bank account, and planned or existing R&D footprint in Canada.
  • Clear commercialization path. Who buys this, when, and at what price — not just technology milestones.
  • Aligned budget and timeline. Funders want realistic project scopes, not wish lists.
  • Strong team narrative. Who executes the project in Canada and how the parent company supports without duplicating work.

What Naru does — and does not do

We help companies identify the right programs, structure eligibility, and prepare application materials alongside your commercialization strategy. We do not guarantee approval. No ethical advisor should. What we do promise is a rigorous, buyer-aware application that reflects how funders actually evaluate submissions — not a generic template copied from another sector.

If non-dilutive funding is part of your North American plan, start with eligibility and narrative before you write a single page of the application.

title: Localization vs. translation: rebuilding your message for North American buyers
author: Naru
excerpt: Translation moves words across languages. Localization moves meaning across markets — and that difference determines whether buyers trust you.
body:
One of the most common failure modes we see in North American market entry is not a weak product — it is a weak message. The website exists. The pitch deck is in English. The sales team has talking points. But the story still reads like it was built for a Korean audience and converted, not composed for a buyer in Toronto, Chicago, or Vancouver.

Translation and localization are not the same thing. Understanding the difference can save months of stalled pipeline.

Translation: accuracy is not enough

Translation converts language. It preserves meaning as faithfully as possible from one tongue to another. That is necessary — but for B2B sales in North America, it is rarely sufficient.

A accurately translated homepage can still fail because:

  • The value proposition leads with technology specs instead of business outcomes
  • Social proof references Korean customers buyers do not recognize
  • Case studies use metrics or framing unfamiliar to local procurement
  • Tone feels formal, distant, or corporate in a market that rewards directness
  • Calls to action are vague (“contact us”) instead of specific (“book a 30-minute pilot scoping call”)

Localization: rebuilding for the buyer

Localization rebuilds your message around how North American buyers actually think, search, evaluate, and buy. The product does not change. The story does.

That includes:

  • Positioning. Reframing from “we are a leading Korean innovator” to “we help [specific buyer] solve [specific problem] faster than [alternative].”
  • Proof points. Swapping domestic references for North American-relevant pilots, certifications, or partnerships — or being honest about early stage while emphasizing transferable results.
  • Visual identity and UX. Layout, imagery, typography, and web patterns that feel native to the market.
  • Sales enablement. One-pagers, decks, and email sequences written for how local reps and buyers actually consume information.

A simple test: the 10-second homepage scan

Show your English homepage to someone in your target industry who has never heard of your company. After ten seconds, they should be able to answer:

  • What does this company do?
  • Who is it for?
  • Why should I care?

If they cannot, you have a localization problem — even if every word is grammatically correct.

Buyers do not reward effort. They reward clarity. Localization is the work of making your value obvious to someone who has no context for where you came from.

Where to start

Do not localize everything at once. Prioritize the assets that touch buyers first:

  1. Homepage hero and one primary conversion path
  2. Core pitch deck (10–12 slides max for first meetings)
  3. One case study or pilot summary — even if the customer is still in Korea, reframe the outcome for a North American reader
  4. LinkedIn company profile and founder narrative

At Naru, localization is not a line item — it is how we make market entry credible. The technology crossed the ocean. The message has to cross the culture.

title: From pilot to pipeline: winning your first North American customer
author: Naru
excerpt: A first pilot proves the product can travel. A pipeline proves the business can. Here is how to design pilots that convert.
body:
Landing a first pilot in North America is a genuine milestone. It validates that a buyer saw enough potential to invest time, budget, and internal political capital. But many expansions quietly stall after that first yes — because the pilot was designed as a one-off experiment, not as the first step in a repeatable sales motion.

The gap between pilot and pipeline is where most international companies lose momentum. Here is how to cross it deliberately.

Why pilots fail to convert

Pilots stall or die when:

  • Success criteria were never defined upfront
  • No executive sponsor owned the outcome internally
  • The pilot scope was too broad (“prove everything”) or too narrow (“free trial with no commitment”)
  • Pricing and rollout path were deferred until “after we see results”
  • Your team treated the pilot as product validation, while the buyer treated it as vendor evaluation

Each of these is fixable at the design stage — not after the pilot ends.

Design every pilot to scale

Before you sign, align on five things in writing:

  • Success metrics. What numbers or outcomes define success? By when?
  • Executive sponsor. Who inside the customer organization will advocate if results are positive?
  • Scope boundaries. What is in, what is out, and what triggers a scope change.
  • Commercial path. If success criteria are met, what happens next — pricing, contract length, rollout geography?
  • Reference rights. Can you name the customer, publish a case study, or introduce them to prospects?

This is not aggressive salesmanship. It is respect for everyone’s time. Buyers appreciate vendors who think in terms of outcomes, not experiments.

From one pilot to a repeatable motion

After your first successful pilot, extract the pattern — not just the testimonial:

  • Which buyer persona said yes fastest?
  • What objection came up most often, and how did you resolve it?
  • How long was the cycle from first meeting to signed pilot?
  • What materials or proof points moved the deal forward?

Turn that into a playbook: target list, outreach sequence, pilot template, and pricing framework. Your second customer should take less time than your first. Your fifth should feel like a system.

When to walk away

Not every pilot is worth taking. Walk away or renegotiate when the buyer will not commit to success criteria, will not assign a sponsor, or expects unlimited free work under the label of “pilot.” Your first North American customer matters — but so does your first bad reference.

A pipeline is not a list of leads. It is a repeatable path from first conversation to signed contract — and pilots are either on that path or off it.

We help companies design GTM motions that treat the first pilot as step one of a pipeline, not a trophy. That is the difference between market access and market success.

title: Friend-shoring and Korea: why North American operators are looking east
author: Naru
excerpt: Supply-chain resilience and allied-nation sourcing are reshaping how North American companies find technology partners — and Korea is on the short list.
body:
Friend-shoring — the practice of relocating supply chains and technology partnerships toward allied nations — is no longer a policy buzzword. It is showing up in procurement criteria, strategic investment mandates, and board-level risk conversations across Canada and the United States.

For Korean innovators, that shift creates a window. For North American operators, it creates a sourcing imperative. Understanding both sides of the dynamic is key to building partnerships that last.

What changed

Three forces converged:

  • Supply-chain risk. Concentration in single regions exposed vulnerabilities in semiconductors, batteries, biotech inputs, and advanced materials.
  • Geopolitical alignment. Governments and enterprises increasingly prefer partners in countries with shared regulatory and security frameworks.
  • Technology depth. Korea’s strength in batteries, displays, robotics, AI applications, biotech manufacturing, and industrial tech is not easily replicated elsewhere.

The result: North American corporates, investors, and government programs are actively looking for credible Korean partners — not as a cost play, but as a capability and resilience play.

What North American buyers actually want

Interest is not the same as trust. Buyers and investors still ask:

  • Can you support us locally — contracts, service, compliance?
  • Do you understand our regulatory environment?
  • Can we pilot before we commit at scale?
  • Who else in North America have you worked with?

Korean companies that answer these questions proactively — with local presence, localized materials, and referenceable progress — convert interest into deals. Those that lead only with technology specs do not.

Opportunity beyond manufacturing

Friend-shoring is not limited to hardware and supply chain. Software, cleantech, healthtech, and AI applications from Korea are entering North American markets where buyers want innovation plus alliance alignment. The framing matters: position as a strategic capability partner, not a low-cost vendor.

The timing argument

Windows like this do not stay open indefinitely. As more Korean companies enter North American markets, differentiation gets harder. Early movers who build local relationships, pilots, and brand presence now become the default partners when procurement accelerates.

Friend-shoring does not guarantee you a customer. It guarantees you a conversation — if you show up ready for one.

Naru exists at that intersection: helping innovators from Korea and Canada build the local credibility, messaging, and execution that turns macro trends into signed deals.

title: Building a fractional growth team instead of hiring five agencies
author: Naru
cover: assets/imgs/blog/Building a fractional growth team instead of hiring five agencies.jpg
excerpt: Early North American expansion rarely justifies a full local team — but a patchwork of agencies creates gaps. There is a third model.
body:
Expanding into North America for the first time presents a staffing paradox. You need senior-level strategy, market knowledge, branding, business development, and ongoing execution — but you cannot yet justify a full local team. So most companies default to agencies: one for the website, one for PR, one for lead gen, one for “strategy.”

Six months later, spend is up, accountability is diffused, and no single party owns the outcome. There is a better model.

The agency patchwork problem

Each vendor optimizes for their slice:

  • The branding agency delivers a beautiful deck — but no pipeline
  • The digital agency launches a site — but no GTM strategy tied to it
  • The BD freelancer opens a few doors — but no follow-through or messaging support
  • The strategy consultant delivers a report — then leaves

You coordinate. You translate between vendors. You become the project manager for your own expansion — on top of running the business at home.

What a fractional growth partner does differently

A fractional growth partner embeds as an extension of your team — not a vendor with a narrow scope. One relationship, one narrative, one owner for the expansion motion across:

  • Market entry strategy and prioritization
  • Positioning, messaging, and sales materials
  • Go-to-market execution and pilot design
  • Partner and customer introductions
  • Funding navigation and program applications
  • Ongoing advisory as traction builds

The model works because accountability is unified. When something is not working — conversion, messaging, pipeline — one team adjusts the whole motion, not just their piece of it.

When fractional makes sense

This model fits best when:

  • You are 6–24 months into a North American expansion
  • Revenue in the market is still emerging but the strategic commitment is real
  • You need senior execution, not junior task work
  • Your HQ team is strong on product but stretched on local GTM

It is less ideal when you only need a one-off asset (a single translation, a logo refresh) with no strategic context — or when you are ready to hire a full local GM and sales team.

How to evaluate a fractional partner

Ask potential partners:

  • What outcomes do you own — not just deliverables?
  • Have you taken companies from first entry to first revenue in this market?
  • How do you work with our HQ team across time zones?
  • What do you do when the strategy needs to change mid-course?
The goal is not to outsource your expansion. It is to embed expertise you do not have yet — without building a department before you have proof.

At Naru Landing, fractional growth partnership is not a retainer label. It is how we work: one integrated team from first validation to lasting traction. Strategy and execution, in one partner.
